text:
"I need one hour. A locked run-of-show for Sunday—logistics, tiers, timings. If I canget the structure on paper tonight, the rest of the weekend stays work. "

"One hour. Then what? "

"Then I go to bed. Alone. With the door locked and the folders in order. "

"You say that like a threat. "

"It's a protocol. "

He nodded, and the nod was respectful in a way that made her nervous, because respect from Marcus Reid felt like a door held open rather than a door closed. She took the elevator to the small business center off the lobby, a room with two computers and a printer that hummed like an old refrigerator. Marcus followed at a distance that was professional by three feet and personal by everything else.

Elena opened her laptop, created a new document, and typed the header: SUNDAY RUN-OF-SHOW. Below it she built the skeleton with the same precision she used for preservation briefs—time, location, personnel, contingency. She had done this a hundred times for pitches, site visits, client presentations. The format was a container. Containers were safe.

"Tier one: arrival and setup, eight to nine. Tier two: rehearsal block, nine to noon. Tier three: break and reset, noon to one. Tier four: performance or broadcast, one to two. Tier five: strike and debrief, two to three. Everything else is unscheduled and therefore unaccounted for. "

"Unaccounted for sounds like a problem you're solving for. "

"Unaccounted for is a problem I'm preventing. "

He pulled a chair to the adjacent computer and opened his notebook, not the laptop, and began sketching something beside her document—not music this time, but a timeline. His handwriting was looser than hers, the lines sloping where hers were level, but the structure was there. She could see it. Time blocks, transitions, the places where one section bled into another. He was building the same skeleton from a different angle.

"You're not using the template. "

"Your template has no room for the unexpected. Sunday has a broadcast, a live audience, and a room that sounds different when it's full. I need to account for the room. "

"The room is documented. I measured it this afternoon. Ceiling height, window placement, absorption coefficients. The room is accounted for. "

"The room on paper is not the room with people in it. "

"That's what the tiers are for. They create buffers. Buffers absorb variance. "

"Buffers also kill momentum. You put a buffer between every feeling and it never lands. "

Elena's fingers paused on the keyboard. The word "feeling" sat between them like a note she had not authorized, and she felt the familiar tension between wanting to erase it and wanting to understand why he had said it. She chose the third option, which was to ignore it and continue.

"Tier two needs sub-blocks. Rehearsal one: ensemble familiarization, nine to ten. Rehearsal two: section work, ten to eleven. Rehearsal three: full run, eleven to noon. Each sub-block has a hard stop. "

"Hard stops are for recordings. Live rooms need soft landings. If the kids are feeling it at eleven-forty-five, you don'tcut them off because the spreadsheet says so. "

"If the spreadsheet doesn'tsay so, nobody knows when to stop. "

"That's the point. Sometimes you stop because the room tells you, not the paper. "

Elena closed her eyes for one second. One second was enough to feel the pull and insufficient to fall into it. When she opened them, Marcus was watching her with that patient attention again, the look that said he had heard the thing she was not saying and was waiting for her to say it anyway.

"I'm not debating the philosophy of time management with you at eight o'clock on a Friday night in a business center. "

"You're not debating. You're defending. There's a difference. "

"The difference is irrelevant. "

"The difference is everything. "

She returned to the document. Her typing had gone faster, the keys sharp and percussive, and she could feel the hour slipping—not because Marcus was distracting her, but because the document was growing beyond its container. She had started with logistics and now found herself writing contingencies for weather delays, for student absences, for the possibility that the broadcast equipment would fail. Each contingency was a letter she had not planned for, and the letters were multiplying.

"I need the broadcast window confirmed. Is it one to two or one-thirty to two-thirty? "

"Rosa said one. She also said she'd know by Saturday morning if the station could push it. "

"So the tier is contingent on a confirmation that doesn't exist yet. "

"Yes. "

"Then I can't lock the run-of-show. "

"No. "

Elena stared at the screen. The document was half-finished, its structure compromised by an unknown she could not control, and the feeling was familiar—it was the same feeling she had at the airport when Vivian Shaw said every flight was cancelled. The contingency list, exhausted. The plan, broken. Except this time there was no letter E to reach for, because the unknown was not a route but a person, and Rosa was not answering her phone.

"This is why I don't collaborate. The plan breaks the moment it depends on someone else's answer. "

"The plan doesn't break. It bends. Bending isn't breaking. "

"Bending is what happens right before breaking. "

"Or right before it finds a shape it couldn't have planned for. "

Elena saved the document and closed the laptop. The hour was up. She had not produced a locked run-of-show, and the failure sat in her chest like a stone she could not file anywhere. Marcus was still in his chair, his notebook open, his timeline sketched in pencil with all the soft landings she had refused to build in.

"I need to go to bed. "

"I know. "

"This isn't—"

"I know what this isn't. "

She stood, and he stood, and they were close in the small room with its humming printer and its fluorescent light that made everything look like evidence. Elena could feel the almost-kiss from last night reforming between them, not as a memory but as a possibility, and the possibility was worse because she had spent an hour proving she could keep things professional and had failed by every metric she had set.

"I'll finish the run-of-show in the morning. Once Rosa confirms the broadcast window. "

"And if she doesn't confirm? "

"Then I'll build two versions. A and B. And I'llrun both. "

"A and B. No C through E? "

"Not tonight. "

He stepped aside to let her pass, and as she moved through the door, his hand brushed her elbow—not a grab, not a hold, just a point of contact so brief it could have been accidental. Elena stopped in the hallway. The fluorescent light from the business center fell across her face, and she could feel the stone in her chest shift, not dissolving but rearranging, making room for something she had not budgeted for.

"Marcus. "

"Yeah. "

"Don't do that. "

"Do what? "

"Make it feel like a chord I didn't authorize. "

He was quiet for a moment, and in the quiet Elena heard the rain and the printer and the distance between them, which was three feet and also everything. When he spoke, his voice was lower, not softer but more careful, as if he were choosing notes from a scale he usually played by feel.

"I'm not trying to make you feel anything. I'm just not going to pretend I don't. "

Elena walked to the elevator. She pressed the button. She did not turn around. The doors opened, and she stepped inside, and as they closed, she saw Marcus Reid still standing in the hallway with his notebook under his arm, looking at the space where she had been with an expression that was not triumph and not sadness but something in between—the face of someone who had heard a melody he couldn't quite place and was going to spend the weekend trying to find it.

In her room, Elena locked the door, set the folders in a row, and sat on the edge of the bed. She opened her phone and found Priya Desai's message from that morning, still unanswered beyond the single word she had sent. She typed: "Stranded through Sunday. Pitch deck section sent. I'm fine. " She stared at it. She deleted "I'm fine. " She sent the first two sentences and put the phone face-down on the nightstand.

The run-of-show sat unfinished on her laptop. The broadcast window was unconfirmed. The weekend stretched ahead like a piece of music she had not written, and Marcus Reid had already begun to rearrange her measures without asking. Elena Marchetti, who had planned for every letter except this one, lay down in her clothes and stared at the ceiling, and the almost-kiss hung in the dark like a note held past its beat—unfinished, unauthorized, impossible to ignore.
